title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams track and manage their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are looking for a self-hosted alternative with more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch from Jira to Plane to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Plane is free and self-hosted, while Jira has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to have full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Jira has a more user-friendly interface.
* Scalability: Jira is more scalable and can handle larger teams, while Plane may require more maintenance as the team grows.
* Integration with Git: Plane has native integration with Git, while Jira requires a separate plugin.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Scalable and reliable
* Integrates with many third-party tools
* Good customer support
* Expensive for large teams
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data
* Native integration with Git
* Customizable
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams that need a scalable and reliable project management tool, and are willing to pay for it. It is also a good choice for teams that need a user-friendly interface and good customer support. Plane is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want full control over their data and are looking for a free and self-hosted solution. It is also a good choice for teams that are already familiar with Git and want a native integration.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your data from Jira.
4. Configure any additional settings or plugins as needed.
5. Test your Plane installation to make sure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and polish. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's search function can be slow for large datasets. However, for small to medium-sized teams that want full control over their data and are looking for a free and self-hosted solution, Plane is a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like resource allocation or Gantt charts.
* Teams that are already familiar with Git and want a native integration.
* Teams that want full control over their data and are looking for a free and self-hosted solution.
* Teams that are currently using Jira and are looking to reduce costs.
* Teams that are looking for a customizable project management tool.

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted. You will need to pay for server costs, but there are no per-user fees.
### Can I import my data from Jira to Plane?
Yes, you can export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane scalable?
Plane can handle small to medium-sized teams, but may require more maintenance as the team grows. Jira is more scalable and can handle larger teams.
### Does Plane have good customer support?
No, Plane is an open-source tool and does not have official customer support. However, there are many online resources and communities available to help with any issues.
### Can I use Plane for large teams?
Not yet, Plane is still in development and may not be suitable for large teams. However, it is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams.
meta_description: Plane, a free self-hosted project management tool, offers more control over data. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Zoom vs Jitsi Meet
comparison_markdown:
# Zoom vs Jitsi Meet (2026)

## Overview
Zoom and Jitsi Meet are video conferencing tools that enable teams to hold virtual meetings and collaborate remotely. This comparison benefits individuals and organizations seeking a reliable and feature-rich platform for their communication needs. The core use case for both tools is virtual meetings, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Zoom offers a free plan with limited features, while Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Jitsi Meet allows users to self-host their servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Zoom stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Jitsi Meet requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while Zoom offers a user-friendly interface for easy setup.
* Scalability: Zoom is designed to handle large-scale meetings and webinars, while Jitsi Meet can also scale but may require more configuration.
* Feature Difference: Zoom offers a built-in recording feature, while Jitsi Meet requires additional setup for recording capabilities.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Zoom | Jitsi Meet |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $13.33+/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $13.33 * 50 = $666.50/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $13.33 * 200 = $2666.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Zoom:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Scalable and reliable
* Offers a wide range of features, including screen sharing and recording
* Integrates with many third-party tools
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Jitsi Meet:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible
* Secure and encrypted
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Zoom is suitable for teams that require a user-friendly and scalable video conferencing solution, especially those who need to host large webinars or meetings. It's ideal for small to medium-sized businesses or individuals who want a hassle-free experience. On the other hand, Jitsi Meet is perfect for organizations that prioritize data security and control, such as government agencies, educational institutions, or companies handling sensitive information. It's also suitable for tech-savvy teams or those with dedicated IT support.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Zoom meeting data and recordings in MP4 format.
2. Set up a Jitsi Meet server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Import your meeting data into Jitsi Meet using the IFrame API or a third-party tool.
4. Configure your Jitsi Meet settings, including authentication and authorization.
5. Test your Jitsi Meet setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Jitsi Meet is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and configure. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Jitsi Meet's mobile app support is still in development, which may affect user experience. However, for teams that value data security and control, Jitsi Meet is a viable alternative to Zoom, and we recommend it for those who are willing to invest time in setup and configuration.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like webinars or large-scale meetings.
* Educational institutions or non-profits that require free or low-cost video conferencing solutions.
* Government agencies or companies handling sensitive information that need full control over their data.
* Tech-savvy teams or those with dedicated IT support that can handle complex setup and configuration.
* Organizations that prioritize data security and encryption above ease of use.

## FAQ
### Can I use Jitsi Meet for large-scale webinars?
Jitsi Meet can handle large-scale meetings, but it may require additional configuration and setup. It's not as straightforward as Zoom's webinar feature.
### Is Jitsi Meet free?
Yes, Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source, with no costs per user.
### Can I self-host Jitsi Meet?
Yes, Jitsi Meet offers a self-hosting option, giving you full control over your data and server configuration.
### Does Jitsi Meet have a mobile app?
Jitsi Meet's mobile app support is still in development, but you can access it through a web browser on your mobile device.
### Can I import my Zoom meeting data into Jitsi Meet?
Yes, you can import your Zoom meeting data into Jitsi Meet using the IFrame API or a third-party tool.

# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Google suite of cloud productivity tools including Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and Calendar. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Nextcloud is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Google Workspace costs $6-$18/user/month; Nextcloud is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Google Workspace is Proprietary; Nextcloud is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Nextcloud can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Nextcloud eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Nextcloud has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$300/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,200/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Google Workspace

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Google Workspace if:** Google Workspace is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Google Workspace in its standard export format, review Nextcloud import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Google Workspace tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Google Workspace, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Google Workspace until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Google Workspace paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Google Workspace to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Google Workspace data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
